title: Misalign@k: Tail-Risk Evaluation of Emergent Misalignment Defenses Under Repeated Sampling

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to provide an evaluation protocol that captures deployment tail-risk of emergent misalignment defenses when users can sample repeatedly. Paper [15] discusses evaluating LLM safety under repeated inference via accelerated prompt stress testing, which aligns with the same objective of assessing safety risks under repeated sampling scenarios. The focus on operational failures under sustained use is substantively equivalent to capturing deployment tail-risk in repeated sampling.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces "Misalign@k," which measures the fraction of prompts yielding at least one misaligned output across k high-temperature samples, with dual-scoring of alignment and coherence for sensitivity analysis. Paper [11] discusses the pass@k metric, which measures the probability of obtaining at least one correct solution in k independent samples. While pass@k is applied to reasoning tasks, the underlying primitive — evaluating outcomes across multiple samples — is equivalent. Additionally, paper [15] uses repeated inference sampling to stress-test safety, which overlaps with the sampling-based mechanism of Misalign@k.

### Evaluation
The evaluation applies the Misalign@k protocol to emergent misalignment defenses (KL regularization, data interleaving) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, with zero false positive rate verified on aligned base models. Paper [15] uses repeated inference sampling to evaluate safety risks under sustained use, which is substantively equivalent in evaluation design. Both contributions assess safety under repeated sampling scenarios, even though the specific defenses and models differ.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM safety evaluation. Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [6], [7], [14], [15], and [23] all address LLM safety evaluation, covering various aspects such as application-level safety, misalignment, robustness, and jailbreak attacks. This domain is well-established in prior work.

**PURPOSE: Identify the mechanism causing defense rankings to flip across labeling criteria.**

The purpose is to explain *why* defense rankings change depending on how outputs are labeled/counted — specifically tracing this to incoherent outputs escaping misalignment detection. Papers [16] and [17] identify that obfuscated gradients cause defenses to give a "false sense of security" and cause attack evaluations to flip/fail, which is thematically related but concerns adversarial robustness evaluation, not safety labeling criteria for LLM defenses. Paper [9] (Slope) also addresses gradient obfuscation causing false security. None of these papers establish the same empirical relationship: that incoherence in model outputs mechanically causes ranking reversals under different labeling criteria for safety defenses. The variables and direction of effect are different.

**MECHANISM: Analyze incoherence rates of defended models to show incoherent outputs mechanically escape misalignment counting under standard metrics.**

This mechanism involves measuring incoherence rates and showing they inflate apparent safety scores. Papers [16]/[17] show that obfuscated gradients cause defenses to appear stronger than they are — a structurally similar primitive (a model behavior that causes evaluation metrics to overestimate safety/robustness). The analogy is close: obfuscated gradients → attacks fail to find adversarial examples → defense looks better than it is; incoherent outputs → misalignment not counted → defense looks safer than it is. This is the same underlying primitive: a model output property that causes standard evaluation metrics to overestimate defense quality. Paper [9] also measures a specific model property (gradient slope) to detect when metrics are being fooled.

**EVALUATION: Interleaving's 18.84% incoherence rate masks underlying misalignment, inflating apparent safety under standard labeling.**

This is a specific quantitative finding about a specific defense method. The evaluation design involves measuring incoherence rates and correlating them with metric inflation. No prior paper uses this specific evaluation design — measuring incoherence rates of LLM safety defenses to explain metric inflation. However, the design of "measure a property of defended model outputs to explain why a metric gives misleading results" is used in [16]/[17] (characteristic behaviors of obfuscated-gradient defenses) and [9] (measuring gradient slope to detect obfuscation). These use the same evaluation design logic: quantify a model property to diagnose metric unreliability.

**DOMAIN: Safety metric analysis.**

Papers [16] and [17] explicitly work in the domain of adversarial defense evaluation and safety metrics for adversarial examples — analyzing whether security metrics accurately reflect true robustness. Paper [9] also works in adversarial robustness evaluation. This is the same general application area of "safety/robustness metric analysis," even if the specific object (LLM safety defenses vs. image classifier adversarial robustness) differs.
